---
title: "Running Jobs on the Cluster"
description: "Submit, monitor, and cancel SLURM jobs on the Engineering School cluster, with example scripts for CPU, conda, and GPU jobs."
---

The [Engineering School cluster](engineering-cluster.qmd) uses
[SLURM](https://slurm.schedmd.com/quickstart.html) to share its compute
nodes. You don't run analyses directly on the login node. You write a short
script that says what resources you need and what to run, and submit it with
`sbatch`. SLURM queues the job and runs it on a compute node when the
resources are free. You can log out while it runs.

To log in and set up SSH keys, see
[Engineering School HPC Cluster](engineering-cluster.qmd#logging-in).

## A first job {#first-job}

Save this as `submit.sh` in your home folder on the cluster:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test             # name shown in the queue
#SBATCH --output=test-%j.out        # output file; %j becomes the job ID
#SBATCH --partition=full            # which partition to use
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1           # number of CPU cores
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL        # email when the job ends or fails
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@uc.cl

python analysis.py
```

Submit it:

```bash
sbatch submit.sh
```

`sbatch` prints the job ID. Anything your program prints goes to the output
file (here `test-<jobid>.out`), not to your terminal. Use `--mail-type=ALL`
to also get an email when the job starts.

Use a script rather than `sbatch` command-line flags. The script records what
you asked for, so you can rerun it.

## Choosing resources {#resources}

- **Partition:** `full`, `512x1024`, or `gpus`. See
  [What's available](engineering-cluster.qmd#partitions) for the hardware,
  and run `sinfo` for the exact names and free nodes.
- **CPUs:** more cores only help if your code runs in parallel, for example
  Python's `multiprocessing`, R's `parallel` or `future` packages, or OpenMP
  in C, C++, or Fortran. Set `--cpus-per-task` to the number of cores your
  code actually uses.
- **Detecting cores in your code:** functions like `parallel::detectCores()`
  in R and `os.cpu_count()` in Python report every core on the node, not the
  ones SLURM gave you. Read the `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` environment variable
  instead:

  ```r
  n_cores <- as.integer(Sys.getenv("SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK", "1"))
  ```

  ```python
  import os
  n_cores = int(os.environ.get("SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK", 1))
  ```

- **Limits:** the DT page lists no time or resource limits, but DT stops jobs
  that take over the cluster.

### Priority

When jobs wait in the queue, SLURM decides which runs next from several
factors:

- **Size:** bigger requests get lower priority.
- **Wait time:** the longer a job waits, the higher its priority.
- **Effective use:** if your past jobs used less than they requested, your
  priority drops. If they used what they requested, it rises.

Asking for 32 cores "just in case" makes your current job wait longer and
lowers the priority of your next ones.

## Interactive sessions {#interactive}

Install packages, build conda environments, compile code, and test scripts
in an interactive session on a compute node, not on the login node:

```bash
srun --partition=full --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 --pty bash
```

Your prompt now runs on a compute node. Type `exit` when you're done to
release the resources.

The DT page tells you to use an interactive session for setup but doesn't
give the command. The one above is standard SLURM. If it doesn't work on the
cluster, ask the help desk and fix this page.

## Python or R with conda {#conda}

There's no shared Python or R setup, so you build your own environments with
conda. The DT page recommends conda and installs it with a Miniconda
installer in your home folder. [Miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge)
is the same idea, with the free conda-forge channel as the default. Compute
nodes have internet access, so run these from an interactive session:

```bash
wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh     # accept the defaults; let it update ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

# Then create an environment per project, for example:
conda create -n my-env python=3.12 pandas
conda create -n r-env r-base r-tidyverse
```

Batch jobs don't load your `~/.bashrc` on their own, so add
`source $HOME/.bashrc` before `conda activate`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=conda-job
#SBATCH --output=conda-job-%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=512x1024
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@uc.cl

source $HOME/.bashrc
conda activate my-env

python analysis.py      # or: Rscript analysis.R
```

## GPU jobs {#gpu}

Use the `gpus` partition and request GPUs with `--gres`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-job
#SBATCH --output=gpu-job-%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=gpus
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                # number of GPUs
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@uc.cl

source $HOME/.bashrc
conda activate my-gpu-env

python train.py
```

A GPU only speeds things up if your code is written to use one, for example
PyTorch or JAX with CUDA. The GPU nodes are shared, so request only what you
use.

## Checking and cancelling jobs {#monitoring}

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `squeue -u $USER` | Your jobs. In the `ST` column, `R` is running and `PD` is pending. |
| `squeue` | Every job on the cluster |
| `sinfo` | Partitions and the state of their nodes |
| `scancel <jobid>` | Cancel one of your jobs |

The DT page also suggests these more detailed views:

```bash
# All jobs with user, ID, partition, name, run time, state, CPUs, and node
squeue -o "%.10u %.10i %.10P %.20j %.11M %.10T %.4C %N" -S -t

# Per node: load, free memory, and CPUs (allocated/idle/other/total)
sinfo -N -o "%.10N %.10O %.10e %.20C"
```

## Other software {#software}

Run `module avail` to see software installed as modules. The DT page
documents:

- **MATLAB R2021a**, without a graphical display. Load it with
  `module load MATLAB/R2021a`, then run a script with
  `matlab -nodisplay -nojvm < script.m`.
- **Gurobi 13.0.0**, with licenses on the cluster, installed through conda.
- **OpenFOAM** 2412 and 2506, and legacy **FEniCS** 2019.

See the [DT page](https://dt.ing.uc.cl/recursos/cluster/) for the
installation steps and example scripts.
